The Mongolian toad Strauchbufo raddei exhibits several notable life-history traits that are shaped by the harsh continental climate of its range. Females that have completed their somatic growth attain a maximum snout-vent length of 8.9 centimeters [Li = 8.9 centimeters], a body size that is matched by adult males which also reach an ultimate SVL of 8.9 centimeters [Li = 8.9 centimeters], although some sources indicate that males tend to be slightly smaller on average. At the point of metamorphosis, emerging females measure approximately 1.4 centimeters  in SVL, reflecting the considerable size increase that occurs during the subsequent juvenile growth phase. The eggs from which these toadlets develop are relatively small, with a diameter of roughly 2 millimeters, and the resulting hatchling emerges at a wet body mass of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This neonatal mass is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by an aquatic developmental environment where yolk reserves must sustain the embryo until the onset of exogenous feeding.

Reproductive activity in Strauchbufo raddei is tightly coupled to seasonal temperature regimes. The same thermal regime also defines the species’ reproductive potential: females typically produce a single clutch each year, with each clutch containing between 1,070 and 6,000 eggs. This annual output, when translated to a per-day basis under these cool conditions, yields a maximum daily reproduction rate of roughly 9.6 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 9.6 eggs per day] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. The modest clutch frequency is typical of bufonids that inhabit regions with short growing seasons.

Post-metamorphic development in this toad proceeds at a deliberate pace under the cool temperatures characteristic of its habitat. This extended maturation interval contrasts with the rapid metamorphic transition itself, which compresses substantial morphological reorganisation into a brief window. The adult body mass ultimately achieved by females after growth cessation is estimated at 87.1 grams [Wwi = 87.1 grams], a value derived from allometric relationships observed in related bufonids. Males, despite their similar SVL, attain a comparable ultimate wet weight of 87.1 grams [Wwi = 87.1 grams], suggesting that sexual dimorphism in this species is expressed more in body proportions than in absolute mass.

Longevity records for Strauchbufo raddei indicate a relatively extended lifespan for a small-bodied anuran, particularly under the cool thermal conditions that slow metabolic processes. At a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the maximum documented lifespan is 14 years [am = 14 years], a figure that aligns with the upper range of survival reported for other Palearctic bufonids. This extended longevity is likely an adaptive response to the unpredictable environments of the Mongolian steppe, where breeding opportunities may be infrequent and a long reproductive window enhances lifetime fitness. The yolk-sac larva emerges from the egg capsule after the incubation period at 10 °C, entering a free-swimming, endotrophic phase that relies entirely on internal yolk reserves until the tadpole’s mouth opens and the trophic switch to exogenous feeding occurs. This developmental sequence underscores the species’ reliance on stable thermal conditions during the critical early stages.

Comparative analysis with other members of the family Bufonidae highlights the relatively modest body size of Strauchbufo raddei. The ultimate snout-vent length of 8.9 centimeters [Li = 8.9 centimeters] recorded for both sexes places this species among the smaller Asian bufonids, a trait that may facilitate thermoregulation in the exposed, semi-arid landscapes it occupies. The wet weight at birth of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] is consistent with an egg diameter of 2 millimeters, a size that represents a trade-off between fecundity and per-offspring investment given the single annual clutch. At 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the age at puberty for females of 2.5 years following metamorphosis [tp = 2.5 years following metamorphosis] is notably protracted, whereas the maximum lifespan of 14 years [am = 14 years] at 10 °C suggests that once maturity is reached, adults enjoy a considerable reproductive tenure that compensates for the delayed onset of breeding.
